title: Why You Should Never Get Between Two Aggressive Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a viral video of a teacher injured while standing between two fighting students, Linsin argues that teachers are under no obligation to physically insert themselves between aggressive, out-of-control students. He frames rising student violence and 'callousness' toward others' well-being as a newer and more dangerous phenomenon than in his earlier decades of teaching, and insists self-protection now carries greater urgency. He offers a three-step protocol for the moment aggression escalates: call for backup immediately using a pre-arranged protocol, position yourself to the side in a 'triangle' rather than directly between combatants, and use calm body language and soft speech to lower the emotional temperature while waiting for help. He closes by tying the ability to de-escalate violence back to everyday classroom management, arguing that students who don't listen to small rules won't listen when things get heated, so consistent management is itself a safety strategy.
points: You are under no obligation to physically stand between two aggressive students; call for backup the moment you notice rising aggression.
If you must intervene, position yourself to the side and perpendicular to the line between the students (a 'triangle'), never directly between them.
Use palms-down gestures, soft but audible speech, and smooth movement to lower the emotional temperature while stalling for help to arrive.
Watch and note what is said and done during a conflict, since one student may be bullying the other.
Classrooms with poor day-to-day management are where violence happens almost exclusively, so consistent management is itself a safety measure.
quotes: The teacher was facing one of the students when the other picked up a chair and threw it. As the chair arced toward the target, it clipped the teacher in the head and upper body.
There is a carelessness—a better word may be callousness—for the well-being of others that I don’t recall seeing in my previous three decades of teaching.
You’re not a martyr. Risking life and limb isn’t part of your job. You’re under no obligation to put yourself in harm’s way to break up a fight.
You must have a protocol to follow without thinking and be assured that help is on the way. Maybe it’s a group text or internal phone call.
From this position, the students can hear you, you’re out of harm’s way, and, most importantly, you’re better able to keep the rest of your class safe and away from the two potential combatants.
Move smoothly, speak softly though loud enough to hear, and use palms-down hand gestures that universally signal ease and calmness.
Violence happens almost exclusively in classrooms with poor classroom management, where temperatures are high and tension palatable nearly all of the time.
